title: Arjuna stands firm
hookLine: Nani's one note, and how Arjuna's story ends
carry: krishna teaches, then leaves the choice to arjuna
tomorrow: Nani won't just say the verse. she sings it. why?

lines: SAY IT LIKE YOU'RE TELLING ME.
cards: After the birthday, a kitchen, late. The card is propped against the fruit bowl. The granddaughter reads the line aloud to her grandmother, slowly, dandas and all.

Nani doesn't correct a single sound. She has one note: now say it like you're telling me, not reading to me. It might be the whole point, because the Gita itself began as words told, friend to friend, in a chariot.

teach.b: Remember where this began: Arjuna's bow slipping from his hand, Arjuna sitting down and saying, I will not fight. Krishna answers him across eighteen chapters. The act is yours, never the fruit.
No one stops acting, so make every act an offering. And near the very end, Krishna does something surprising. He doesn't command.
He says: I've told you this wisdom; reflect on it fully, then do as you choose. Then he asks: have you heard this with a focused mind? Is your confusion gone?

teach.h: MY CONFUSION IS GONE. I STAND FIRM.
teach.b: And Arjuna answers: my confusion is gone, my memory has come back, my doubts are cleared; I stand firm, and I'll do as you say.
That's the shape of the Gita, and many teachers say it's part of why Hindus love it: a teaching given by a friend, heard, thought through, and then chosen.
Look at everything these two weeks held to get one line said well. Ganesha writing only what he understood. Om before the prayer.
Speech that's true and kind. A word heard before it's read. Nani's note gathers them up: the line isn't for reading at someone.
It's for telling, the way Krishna told it, to someone you love, and then living by.

how: Hindu children often learn a verse by hearing an elder or teacher say it, repeating it back, and only later reading it; a family member may correct the sounds and then, as Nani does here, the way it is said. Many teachers point to Gita 18.63 to show that the Gita ends by asking for reflection and free choice.

games.q: how the story ends — tap the pairs.
p: my doubts are gone; i stand firm

s: Krishna ends the Gita by ordering Arjuna to obey without thinking
he says: reflect on it fully, then do as you choose.
Arjuna's last words in the Gita say his confusion is gone
he stands firm, ready to act.
the Vedas are called shruti because they were first read in books

games.q: at a family dinner a cousin says the Gita is just a god giving orders. what's a fair answer?
o: Krishna teaches, then tells Arjuna to reflect fully and choose.
yes: Arjuna never had any say in it.
the Gita has no teaching, only a battle story.
games.why: reflect on this fully, then do as you choose. and Arjuna, his doubts gone, chooses to stand and act.

practice: Pick one line you love, from a prayer, a verse, a song, and say it aloud once as if reading it off a page. Then say it again as if you were telling it to someone sitting right across from you, someone you'd want it to help.
Sit with the difference, and with the line, for the rest of the time.

wordCard.voice: The sounds: throat to lips, little breath and great, om before the prayer, heard first, and then said to someone.

orig.note: Sanskrit: having reflected; Krishna's word to Arjuna near the Gita's end.

carryVoice: For the road: Krishna teaches, then leaves the choice to Arjuna, and Arjuna stands. Two weeks, done.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 18.63 ('reflect on this fully, then do as you wish'), 18.72–18.73 (Arjuna: delusion gone, memory regained, I stand firm)
